summary: Describes Cisco's Layer Two Forwarding protocol, which tunnels the link layer of higher-level protocols, such as HDLC, async HDLC or SLIP frames. It is a historic protocol and was a forerunner of later tunneling standards.

eli5.summary: A secret tunnel for carrying one kind of network traffic inside another so it can travel far. It is an old idea now mostly history.

questions: what udp port does l2f use
what is a home gateway in l2f
subtitle: Cisco's way to carry a dial-up user's link-layer frames through a tunnel to a gateway somewhere else.

tldr.problem: An ISP's access server answers the phone call, but the user's company wants the dial-up connection to end on its own network, with its own addresses, authentication and protocols.
tldr.mechanism: L2F wraps the user's PPP or SLIP frames in a small L2F header and forwards them through a tunnel from the ISP's Network Access Server to the Home Gateway, using a Multiplex ID to tell the users in the tunnel apart.
tldr.outcome: The user looks as if they dialed straight into the Home Gateway. The RFC itself is a Historic document and does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 2341 is marked Historic and was published as a description of Cisco's protocol, not as an Internet standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Virtual Dial-Up and Why It Is Needed
sections.content:
Traditional dial-up service on the Internet is for registered IP addresses only. Virtual dial-up is a newer class of service that allows several protocols and unregistered IP addresses, for example privately addressed IP, IPX and AppleTalk over SLIP or PPP, across the existing Internet infrastructure.

The RFC lists what the end user wants: no special software on the remote system or home hosts, authentication as in a normal dial-up (PPP CHAP or PAP, TACACS+ and RADIUS, smart cards and one-time passwords), addresses assigned by the home site rather than the ISP, authorization managed by the home site, and accounting at both the ISP and the user's side.

The ISP only does enough authentication to learn who the user claims to be, and so which Home Gateway to contact. The Home Gateway then accepts or rejects the connection. Because third parties might try to open tunnels to a Home Gateway, tunnel setup includes an ISP-to-Home Gateway authentication phase. The RFC's Security Considerations section points back to this discussion.
sections.eli5: The company wants to be the one who checks who you are and gives you your address, even though the phone company's local office picked up the call. The tunnel lets the company stay in charge.

sections.title: How a Virtual Dial-Up Call Works
sections.content:
A remote user dials into the ISP's Network Access Server (NAS) over the telephone network or ISDN, and a PPP link comes up. The NAS looks only at the username in the CHAP or PAP exchange to decide whether the user needs virtual dial-up. The RFC expects, but does not require, structured usernames such as littlewo@cisco.com. The ISP may instead keep a database mapping users to a Home Gateway.

If no tunnel to that gateway exists, the NAS creates one. L2F only needs a medium that offers packet-oriented point-to-point connectivity, such as UDP, Frame Relay PVCs or X.25 VCs. The NAS then allocates an unused Multiplex ID, and sends a connect notification. For CHAP it includes the challenge, username and raw response; for PAP or text dialogs it includes the username and clear text password. For PPP it may also include the LCP CONFACKs, which lets the Home Gateway skip a second round of authentication and LCP negotiation.

If the gateway accepts, it creates a virtual interface as it would for a direct-dialed connection. Frames from the user are stripped of link framing and transparency bytes, wrapped in L2F and forwarded. The gateway unwraps them and handles them as normal incoming frames, and the reverse path works the same way.
sections.eli5: The phone company's office only reads your name tag to find out which company you belong to. Then it passes your call along the pipe, and the company's own front desk decides whether to let you in.

sections.title: The L2F Packet
sections.content:
An L2F packet is an L2F header, the payload (a PPP or SLIP packet) and an optional checksum. The first 16 bits hold the flag bits F, K, P, S and C, plus a 3-bit Ver field that MUST be 001. Then come the Protocol, an optional Sequence number, the Multiplex ID, the Client ID, the Length, and the optional Offset and Key.

The Protocol field is 0x01 for L2F management packets, 0x02 for PPP and 0x03 for SLIP (0x00 is illegal). Sequence numbers are present when the S bit is set, which MUST be the case for all management packets. They start at 0 and count modulo 256. A packet whose number falls in the last value or its 127 successors is silently discarded as a duplicate.

The Multiplex ID (MID) names one connection inside the tunnel, and MID 0 is reserved for the tunnel itself, so only management packets may use it. The Client ID (CLID) helps endpoints sort out interleaved tunnels, and packets with an unknown CLID MUST be silently discarded. The Key, when the K bit is set, is the four 32-bit words of the 128-bit authentication response XORed together, and packets with the wrong key are silently discarded to resist spoofing. The optional checksum is a 16-bit CRC (FCS-16) over the whole packet, and the P bit marks priority packets such as PPP keepalives.

When PPP is encapsulated, flags, transparency data (ACCM or bit stuffing) and the CRC are not carried, but the address and control bytes (unless negotiated away) and the protocol value are. SLIP has its framing and transparency characters removed.
sections.eli5: Each wrapped frame gets a small label saying what kind of thing is inside, which of the many callers it belongs to, and a secret stamp so strangers cannot slip fake mail into the pipe.

sections.title: Setting Up the Tunnel and Each Client
sections.content:
Tunnel setup happens on MID 0 with management packets. The NAS sends L2F_CONF with its name, a random challenge and an Assigned_CLID, with Key and CLID set to 0. The Home Gateway answers with its own L2F_CONF containing its name, its own challenge and its own Assigned_CLID. After that each side tags packets with the CLID the peer assigned.

Both sides then send L2F_OPEN carrying a CHAP-style MD5 response to the other side's challenge, and the 32-bit Key derived from it is used on every later packet for the life of the tunnel. An L2F_OPEN with a wrong response during tunnel setup MUST be silently discarded, and logging it is recommended.

To add a user, the NAS sends an L2F_OPEN on a new, non-zero MID. It carries the authentication type (CHAP, PAP, textual SLIP login or none), the name, challenge and response, and optionally copies of the LCP packets. The gateway accepts by sending an L2F_OPEN back with no sub-options, or declines with L2F_CLOSE. After that PPP or SLIP frames flow in both directions.

Packets with an invalid Key are dropped but do not trigger a tunnel close. The RFC says this prevents denial-of-service attacks.
sections.eli5: First the two ends swap secret questions and prove they know the same password. Only then do they start letting individual callers through the pipe, one numbered seat at a time.

sections.title: Management Messages
sections.content:
A management packet body is zero or more options. Each option is a one-byte message type followed by sub-options. The types are L2F_CONF, L2F_OPEN, L2F_CLOSE, L2F_ECHO and L2F_ECHO_RESP. A message of the Invalid type, an unknown option, or any illegal packet makes the receiver discard it and request an L2F_CLOSE of the whole tunnel.

L2F_CLOSE can be sent by either side at any time. With MID 0 it ends the whole tunnel, and with a non-zero MID it ends one client. From the Home Gateway in reply to an L2F_OPEN it means the connection was declined. Its L2F_CLOSE_WHY sub-option is a 32-bit mask of reasons, and L2F_CLOSE_STR adds a descriptive ASCII string. An implementation may choose not to report a reason such as unknown user, since that can be used to probe the user name space.

L2F_ECHO is optional, with MID 0. If used, no more than one request per second may be sent, the payload MUST be 64 bytes or less, and at least 5 unanswered echoes are recommended before assuming the peer is gone. Every implementation MUST answer with L2F_ECHO_RESP.
sections.eli5: The messages are like a few simple phrases: here is my name tag, you may come in, goodbye (with a reason), and are you still there? Everyone has to answer the last one.

sections.title: Delivery, State Tables and UDP
sections.content:
L2F is designed for unreliable point-to-point links. It does not do flow control or reliable delivery of user data; each tunneled protocol is expected to handle that itself. Only control messages are retransmitted, and they are exchanged lock-step. The RFC gives state tables for the NAS and the Home Gateway, for both the tunnel and each client, with retry timeouts numbered 1-3 and then a fourth timeout that cleans up.

L2F does not look inside the tunneled frames, so PPP features such as compression, multilink or encryption work between the user and the Home Gateway, and PPP termination is just another tunneled frame. The gateway turns a PPP hang-up into an L2F_CLOSE.

Over IP, the whole L2F packet travels in a UDP datagram using the well-known port 1701 for both source and destination, with CLID values doing the demultiplexing. The source IP address for a given CLID may change during a connection, and replies should use the last source address seen. L2F does nothing special about IP fragmentation.
sections.eli5: The pipe does not promise every parcel arrives. Only the little control notes get re-sent if lost, and the people at each end of the call take care of the rest themselves.
